title: Answer what was actually said
summary: Learn the flow, the two column page that keeps an argument honest, then take a machine's constructive apart in ninety seconds without inventing a single word it did not say.
materials: one sheet of paper turned landscape, and a pen that keeps up
the 2 minute and 1 minute sand timers
laptop with the AI, used with a grown up in the room

steps.title: The flow, and the rule it protects
steps.body:
Here is the most common way a debate is lost. Somebody stands up and answers the argument they expected, or the argument they had already prepared, or the argument they wish the other side had made. Meanwhile the argument that was actually made is still standing there, untouched, and the judge can see it.

The cure is a page. Turn a sheet sideways and draw a line down the middle. The left column is theirs: every point they make, one short line each, in the order they make them, with a gap under each one. The right column is yours: your answer to each point, written straight across from the point it answers. That page is called a flow, and it is the single most useful object in a debate. When you speak, you read across the rows. Their point, your answer. Their next point, your answer. Nothing gets missed, because a blank space in the right column is visible from across the room.

Three rules for filling it in. Write short: three or four words a line, not sentences, or the next point goes past while you are still writing this one. Write what they said, using their own words where you can, not your improved version of it. And leave the gaps, because your answers arrive later than their points do, and they need somewhere to land.

The steelman rule from last season is still standing, and the flow is what makes it possible. Before you knock a point down, say it back so well that they would nod. You cannot do that from memory. You can do it from a page.

This week's motion, which a machine will argue and you will answer: everything you make should be given away for free. You just put your own code on the internet where anybody can read it, and in a few weeks you are going to sell something to people who owe you nothing. You have a real stake in both sides of this, which is exactly why it is worth arguing.

And carry this one into your recording at the end: if nobody buys a thing, was it worth making?

steps.title: Flow the machine
steps.body:
Set the page up before a single word is spoken. Landscape, line down the middle, their side on the left, yours on the right. Number the rows down the left column, so you can say the number out loud later and everyone knows exactly which point you mean.

Now ask the AI, with a grown up nearby, for a two minute constructive speech arguing for the motion: everything you make should be given away for free. Ask for exactly three points, each with a claim and one reason, and ask it to read at a normal speaking speed rather than dumping the text on the screen. Do not read ahead. The whole skill this week is catching things at the speed a person actually talks.

Flow it as it speaks. One line per point, three or four words. If you miss something, leave the row blank and keep up rather than stopping to repair it. A gap you can see is better than a page you fell behind on.

When it finishes, take twenty seconds and read your left column back. Any row that you cannot understand from your own note is a row you wrote too slowly or too cleverly. Fix those two rows now, while it is fresh, and notice what you did differently on the rows that came out clean.
checklist: The page was drawn, split and numbered before the speech started
Every point the machine made has its own numbered row on the left
The notes are short lines in its words, not my improved version of its words
I stayed with the speech instead of stopping to repair a row I missed

steps.title: Ninety seconds, straight back
steps.body:
You get ninety seconds, and there are three points against you. That is thirty seconds each, which is not enough to be thorough, so choose. Mark the two rows you can genuinely beat and the one you will leave for later. Choosing what to drop is a skill, not a retreat.

Fill the right column for the two you picked. Each answer is three short beats: their point said back fairly, then the word but, then your reason. Write the beats as notes, never as a script, because a script read aloud sounds like a script read aloud.

Then signpost, so the judge never has to guess where you are. On their first point, that giving work away is what makes it useful, they are right that it spreads further. But. Then your reason. Then: on their second point. Saying the number and the point before you answer it is what tells a judge you are answering rather than talking.

Run the minute sand timer plus thirty seconds on a clock, or ask a grown up to give you the ninety. The timer is the referee both sides share, so finishing inside it is part of the job and not a punishment. Deliver it standing, from the flow, looking up. Then run it once more, and notice that the second run is always shorter and calmer than the first.
checklist: I picked two points to answer and said out loud which one I was dropping and why
Each answer starts by saying their point back fairly before it gets knocked down
I signposted which numbered point I was on before every answer
I spoke from notes and the flow, never from a written out script
The rebuttal finished inside ninety seconds

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record your ninety second rebuttal in one take, standing, with the flow page in your hand. Hold the page up to the camera at the start so both columns are visible. Then, in the same recording, answer this week's question: if nobody buys a thing, was it worth making, and what is your reason?
